title: Even 10 Minutes of “Slow Running” Can Give Your Brain a Boost - Nautilus
gist: A new study in Imaging Neuroscience reportedly finds that a very small dose of exercise — on the order of 10 minutes of slow running — is enough to produce measurable cognitive benefit, reframing the exercise-and-brain question as one of minimum effective dose.

insights.claim: A new study published in the journal Imaging Neuroscience finds that the amount of exercise needed to obtain cognitive benefit is very little — on the order of 10 minutes of slow running.
insights.so_what: A very low exercise threshold expands the addressable market for movement-based wellness products from athletes to the sedentary majority.
insights.quote: According to a new study published in the journal Imaging Neuroscience, it’s actually very little.
insights.locator: According to a new study published in the journal
insights.speaker: Jake Currie

insights.claim: The right research question about exercise and the brain is not how much is optimal but how little one can get away with before reaping cognitive rewards.
insights.so_what: Dose-minimization framing is how adherence-driven health products get designed; it favors low-friction offerings over high-commitment programs.
insights.quote: How little exercise can we get away with before we reap some of these rewards?
insights.locator: So the question on every, shall we say
insights.speaker: Jake Currie

insights.claim: Exercise-and-cognition studies use different methodologies and reach different conclusions, but the growing body of work converges on the claim that at least some movement delivers some cognitive and psychological benefit.
insights.so_what: Treat headline effect sizes in this field skeptically; the durable signal is directional, not magnitude-specific.
insights.quote: While different studies using different methodologies may come to different conclusions, it’s become clear that at least some movement offers some cognitive and psychological benefits.
insights.locator: There’s a growing pile of research
insights.speaker: Jake Currie

insights.claim: The article attributes the brain boost from slow running to the head bob of the running motion itself rather than to cardiovascular load.
insights.so_what: If mechanical head motion rather than aerobic intensity drives the effect, low-intensity movement modalities would carry the same benefit.
insights.quote: It’s all in the head bob
insights.speaker: Jake Currie
